text:
Jordan Lee: Dropping the ADR draft for RBAC v2 policy eval semantics here: https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/ARCH/ADR-014+-+RBAC+v2+policy+format (WIP). Main open question: do we support explicit `deny` rules with deny-overrides, or keep it allow-only (default deny) for v1? This affects debugging + audit evidence.

Confluence Bot: Unfurl: ADR-014 - RBAC v2 policy format (Draft)

Kaitlyn Nguyen: thanks. I’m +1 on deciding this now vs punting. We’re already wiring reason codes in the middleware and it changes what we log.

Ethan Park: fwiw control plane prefers simplest thing that’s hard to misuse. allow-only feels safer / fewer footguns.

Marcus Lin: security angle: explicit deny can be useful for incident response (“block action X for everyone except Y”) and for least-privilege when you have broad allow at org scope but want to carve out specific actions.

Allison Grant: logging/debuggability: deny-overrides tends to be *harder* to explain to humans. “you have allow A via role1 but denied via role2 because deny matched” is a nightmare unless we build a real explain trace.

Jordan Lee: yeah that’s exactly the worry. In draft I outlined two options:
1) allow-only: decision = allow if any statement matches; else deny
2) deny-overrides: decision = deny if any deny matches; else allow if any allow matches; else deny

Chloe Martin: console UX: if we have deny rules, people will ask “where did that deny come from” in UI. We don’t have a surface to show per-statement trace yet.

Benji Okafor: also role composition: we’re going to have multiple roles per user (default + custom + possibly SSO group mapping). deny-overrides adds a whole new class of “surprising” outcomes.

Marcus Lin: but allow-only forces you to avoid granting broad privileges in the first place, which is good. the carve-out use case can be handled with better role design (don’t grant it, instead grant narrowly).

Ethan Park: incident response case can be handled outside policy semantics too. e.g. a server-side “emergency blocklist” keyed by action/resource that short-circuits. That keeps policy format clean.

Allison Grant: +1. If we *do* want emergency deny, it should be operationally controlled and loudly logged, not something that can accidentally ship in a bundle.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: agree. plus for Private deployments, policy bundle updates can lag (air-gapped). relying on “ship deny” for incident response isn’t great anyway.

Connor O'Brien: from migration/release side: allow-only reduces risk in dual-eval. If we introduce denies, shadow mode will show a bunch of “denied due to deny-statement you didn’t know existed” issues. Hard to reason about diff vs RBAC v1.

Jordan Lee: question: do we foresee a real enterprise requirement for explicit denies in policy *format*? (not emergency tooling)

Marcus Lin: questionnaires sometimes say “can you explicitly restrict X even if user is admin” but that’s more about SoD + not having “super-admin” for everything. If we keep Org Admin powerful, they’ll ask for custom roles + separation, not explicit denies.

Chloe Martin: for UI we can implement “effective permissions” by union of allows relatively easily (still non-trivial but doable). Adding denies means we need to show precedence + conflicts.

Allison Grant: audit log spec wants `decision_reason` and references to policy version + role ids. With deny-overrides we’d also need `matched_deny_statements` (or at least ids) to make it explainable.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: we can still do explainability with allow-only: log `matched_allow_statement_ids` (maybe sampled / size-capped) and a canonical reason code:
- `ALLOW_MATCH`
- `DENY_NO_MATCH`
- `DENY_SCOPE_MISMATCH`
That’s already helpful.

Ethan Park: what about “deny by default” + “deny overrides” confusion? People might read deny-overrides as “deny unless explicitly allowed” which is already true.

Jordan Lee: yeah. terminology aside, explicit deny is the extra feature.

Marcus Lin: I’m ok with allow-only + default deny, provided we have:
1) a way to quickly revoke access (disable role assignment / user / API key) and
2) support-only/break-glass is not expressed as “deny everyone, allow support” in the same policy.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: re (2) we’re planning break-glass as a separate elevated session + separate actor type w/ its own policy bundle section. So we can avoid mixing.

Allison Grant: +1. Also recommend ADR include a “future extension” note: we can add deny statements later, but only if we also commit to an explain API and UI support.

Connor O'Brien: and we should be explicit that adding deny statements later is a format version bump (`policy_schema_version`), so Private can handle skew.

Benji Okafor: perf: evaluation with explicit denies may require scanning more statements (unless we index). Not huge, but we’re trying to keep authz on hot paths cheap.

Jordan Lee: ok sounds like consensus forming: allow-only (default deny) for RBAC v2 v0.1 policy format. Any objections?

Marcus Lin: no objection. Please add the “operational emergency blocklist” note so security has an answer for IR.

Chloe Martin: +1. and call out UX implication: without denies, “effective permission” is monotonic with added roles, which is easier to explain.

Allison Grant: +1. For audit logs, we should standardize reason codes now and add a deterministic “explain string” (human readable) for denied decisions. Even a short one like `missing_permission: org.audit.export`.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: I’ll update middleware to emit `missing_permission` when deny due to no match, and keep `policy_version`, `role_ids`, `action`, `resource`, `scope`.

Jordan Lee: action items:
- I’ll update ADR-014: choose allow-only semantics, add rationale + future deny extension notes.
- Allison: can you drop proposed reason code list in the doc comments?
- Kaitlyn: please sanity check the logging fields vs Kevin’s audit log spec.

Allison Grant: yep will do. (also adding note: if we ever add deny statements, we must log statement ids to avoid “opaque deny”.)

Marcus Lin: :thumbsup: also please add a line about “deny by default at every layer” (gateway and service) so we don’t accidentally rely on client-side checks.

Jordan Lee: noted. Updating today.

Connor O'Brien: thanks. ping me when ADR is updated; I’ll link it in the ENG-5389 rollout playbook so we stop re-litigating this during launch.
